citation: Nomi, T., & Allensworth, E. (2009). "Double-Dose" Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation: Effects on Students' Academic Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 2(2), 111-148. doi:10.1080/19345740802676739 (ERIC EJ866973)
design: regression discontinuity combined with interrupted time series; instrumental variables
population_location: Chicago Public Schools, first-time 9th graders below national median on 8th-grade ITBS math, 2003 cohort onward
program_model: Double-period algebra: regular Algebra I plus a second support algebra period (school schedule policy)
outcome_measure: 9th-grade algebra test scores (end-of-year PLAN/EXPLORE-type tests), grades, failure rates; 10th-grade geometry
direction: positive on test scores; little on grades and failure
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Providing support courses improved algebra test scores for the target population but only modestly affected grades and failure rates. Students with very low initial abilities benefited less than students close to the national median.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Same policy as Cortes et al. 2015 and Nomi & Allensworth 2013 / Nomi & Raudenbush 2016; these are one natural experiment, not independent replications.

citation: Cortes, K. E., Goodman, J. S., & Nomi, T. (2015). Intensive Math Instruction and Educational Attainment: Long-Run Impacts of Double-Dose Algebra. Journal of Human Resources, 50(1), 108-158. doi:10.3368/jhr.50.1.108 (NBER WP 20211; ERIC ED563067 is the 2013 SREE version)
population_location: Chicago Public Schools, 2003 and 2004 9th-grade cohorts, ~11,000 students, 95% low-income Black or Hispanic
program_model: Double-dose algebra (two periods of algebra in 9th grade)
outcome_measure: Test scores, credits, high school graduation, college enrollment
effect_as_reported: NBER abstract: 'A regression discontinuity design shows substantial positive impacts of double-dose algebra on credits earned, test scores, high school graduation and college enrollment rates. Test score effects under-predict attainment effects.' SREE version: share earning at least a B in freshman algebra +9.4 percentage points; algebra pass rate +4.7 pp, not significant.
notes: school model, not a partner link. Lead from task confirmed. Effect largest for students with below-average reading skills. Gives S4 evidence too (graduation), already a lane-2-to-S4 pathway.

citation: Nomi, T., & Allensworth, E. M. (2013). Sorting and Supporting: Why Double-Dose Algebra Led to Better Test Scores but More Course Failures. American Educational Research Journal, 50(4), 756-788. doi:10.3102/0002831212469997 (ERIC EJ1014932)
design: regression discontinuity and mechanism analyses (same Chicago policy)
population_location: Chicago 9th graders
program_model: Double-dose algebra
direction: mixed (tests up, failures up for above-average students)
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'This led to higher test scores for students with both above- and below-average skills, yet failure rates increased for above-average students.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Same natural experiment as K1 double-dose rows; do not count as an independent study.

citation: Nomi, T., & Raudenbush, S. W. (2016). Making a Success of "Algebra for All": The Impact of Extended Instructional Time and Classroom Peer Skill in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 38(2), 431-451. doi:10.3102/0162373716643756 (ERIC EJ1100477)
design: regression discontinuity with school-specific instrumental variables
population_location: Chicago 9th graders
program_model: Double-dose algebra; moderation by classroom peer skill
direction: conditional: positive where median-skill students were not placed in low-skill classrooms; little or none otherwise
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'the Double-Dose policy had little or no effect for median-skill students in schools that exposed them to low-skill classrooms. However, the effects of Double Dose were substantially positive in schools that did not do so.'
proposed_tier: Tested (school model); condition on the claim
notes: school model, not a partner link. Condition: extra time works when it does not track students into low-skill classes.

citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. doi:10.3102/0162373709343471 (ERIC EJ866927)
design: interrupted time-series cohort design with multiple comparisons
population_location: Chicago 9th graders, 1997 policy
program_model: Ending remedial math; Algebra I for all 9th graders (no extra time)
outcome_measure: Test scores, failure rates, grades, college entry
direction: null on tests; negative on failure
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'failure rates increased, grades slightly declined, test scores did not improve, and students were no more likely to enter college.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Null for course access without support; contrasts with double-dose.

citation: Taylor, E. (2014). Spending more of the school day in math class: Evidence from a regression discontinuity in middle school. Journal of Public Economics, 117, 162-181. doi:10.1016/j.jpubeco.2014.06.002
population_location: Miami-Dade middle school students (grades 6-8)
program_model: Required second (remedial) math class
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Math achievement grows much faster under the requirement, 0.16-0.18 student standard deviations. Yet, one year after returning to a regular one-class schedule, the initial gains decay by as much as half, and two years later just one-third of the initial treatment effect remains.'
proposed_tier: Out of lane 1 (middle school test); context on fadeout
notes: school model, not a partner link. Recorded because it bounds double-dose claims: extra-time gains fade. Not a high school course outcome.

citation: Tidd, S. T., Stoelinga, T. M., Bush-Richards, A. M., De Sena, D. L., & Dwyer, T. J. (2018). An Intensification Approach to Double-Block Algebra: A Pilot Implementation of Intensified Algebra in A Large Urban School District. Journal of Educational Research, 111(3). doi:10.1080/00220671.2016.1209454 (ERIC EJ1161560)
design: pilot comparison (design details not in abstract; effect reported for high-fidelity implementers)
population_location: Large urban district (Texas suggested by state EOC; not confirmed)
program_model: Intensified Algebra I double-block curriculum (Agile Mind / Dana Center)
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'when implemented with fidelity, participation in the program significantly increased student achievement on the state end-of-course algebra I assessment.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Evidence for ESSA lists Intensified Algebra as 'No studies met inclusion requirements'.

citation: MDRC (2026). Expanding High-Dosage Tutoring [evaluation of Saga Education's live-online tutoring model in eight New York City high schools, 2021-22 to 2023-24].
design: quasi-experimental matched comparison (students in comparable NYC high schools)
population_location: New York City, 9th graders, 8 high schools
program_model: Saga high-dosage math tutoring delivered live online
outcome_measure: NY State Algebra I Regents exam passing and score by end of 9th grade; math GPA
effect_as_reported: MDRC page: 'Students who received tutoring using the model were more likely to pass the standardized state Algebra I Regents Exam by the end of ninth grade (39 percent compared with 31 percent for the comparison group), they had higher Regents Exam scores, and they earned higher math grade point averages'
proposed_tier: Tested (adds an end-of-course exam outcome to L-03); QED only
already_screened: partly: Saga model in L-03 / S-0246 / S-0282, but this NYC online evaluation and its Regents Algebra I outcome are not recorded there
notes: Directly relevant: an Algebra I end-of-course exam (Regents) outcome for a partner-delivered tutoring model. Weaker for boys and very low entering levels. Need full report citation, authors and baseline-equivalence check.

citation: Bhatt, M. P., Guryan, J., Khan, S. A., LaForest-Tucker, M., & Mishra, B. (2024). Can Technology Facilitate Scale? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation of High Dosage Tutoring. NBER Working Paper 32510.
population_location: Two large districts (Chicago and New York City), 2018-19 and 2019-20, high school
program_model: Saga hybrid tutoring: groups of four, 2 with in-person tutor and 2 on computer-assisted learning, alternating days
effect_as_reported: NBER abstract: 'We find gains in students' math standardized test scores of 0.23 standard deviations for participating students'; per-pupil costs 'approximately 30 percent lower than the 2-to-1 tutoring model'
already_screened: S-0282; listed as a key study for Saga on Evidence for ESSA
notes: Record only to confirm L-03 cites it; a lower-cost model replicating the effect.

citation: Fryer, R. G., Jr. (2014). Injecting Charter School Best Practices into Traditional Public Schools: Evidence from Field Experiments. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 129(3), 1355-1407. doi:10.1093/qje/qju011 (NBER WP 17494)
design: school-level randomized field experiment plus quasi-experimental comparisons
population_location: Houston (Apollo 20), 20 low-performing schools incl. 4 high schools; Denver and Chicago comparisons
program_model: Bundle: extended time, staff replacement, high-dosage math tutoring (6th and 9th grade), data use, expectations
direction: positive in math, null in reading
effect_as_reported: QJE abstract: 'significantly increases student math achievement in treated elementary and secondary schools-by 0.15 to 0.18 standard deviations a year-and has little effect on reading achievement.'
proposed_tier: Tested (school model bundle); high school estimate needs the paper
notes: school model, not a partner link (whole-school bundle). Tutoring effect not separated from bundle in abstract; check high-school-specific estimates in paper.

citation: Cook, M. A., & Ross, S. M. (2023). Impact Evaluation of Intervene K-12 Tutoring on Grade 9 Mathematics Achievement in Hartford Public Schools. Johns Hopkins Center for Research and Reform in Education (ERIC ED659897).
population_location: Hartford, CT, Grade 9 English learners recently arrived, small sample
program_model: Intervene K-12 tutoring (provider-delivered)
outcome_measure: End-of-course Algebra I exam; PSAT math
direction: positive on EOC (ES ~0.40); PSAT not significant
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Treatment students outgained matched comparison students on the EOY Algebra I exam by more than 7 points... these impacts did not reach statistical significance... The effect size of the EOC Algebra I score impact was nearly 0.40 SDs'
proposed_tier: Below the bar (single small QED, district EOC; significance unclear)
notes: Evidence for ESSA lists Intervene K-12 as 'No Evidence' ('Qualifying studies found no significant positive results'). Abstract wording on significance is ambiguous.

citation: Deacon, G., & Chojnacki, G. (2023). Impacts of UPchieve On-Demand Tutoring on Students' Math Knowledge and Perceptions. Middle Years Math Grantee Report Series. Mathematica (ERIC ED628646).
design: pilot randomized encouragement trial (incentives to use more tutoring)
population_location: 9th and 10th graders in Title I schools who signed up for UPchieve, US
program_model: Free online on-demand tutoring by unpaid volunteers
direction: null at conventional significance (positive point estimate)
effect_as_reported: Report: 'students scoring 9 percentile points higher on the Star Math assessment... not statistically significant according to a conventional statistical test (p = 0.12)... 0.23 standard deviations'
proposed_tier: Null/below the bar (pilot; contrast is more vs less usage)
notes: Volunteer online model; self-selected students. Do not claim.

citation: Hamlin, D., et al. (2023). Transformative Tutoring Initiative, University of Oklahoma [randomized study of high-dosage math tutoring for 9th graders]. OU news release.
design: randomized (two-year; tutoring vs remedial math course)
population_location: Oklahoma City and Norman area high schools, 194 low-achieving 9th graders
program_model: University students as tutors, 1 tutor to 2 students, 50 minutes 3 times a week, in school day
effect_as_reported: lead: release quotes interim gains 'more than double that of their peers in the control group'; no effect size or report located
notes: Find the technical report or paper before any use.

citation: Kraft, M. A. (2015). How to Make Additional Time Matter: Integrating Individualized Tutorials into an Extended Day. Education Finance and Policy, 10(1), 81-116.
population_location: Boston MATCH charter high school
program_model: Full-time tutors in extended day
effect_as_reported: lead (not re-fetched; see S-0049)
notes: Listed for completeness; no new information.

citation: Pane, J. F., Griffin, B. A., McCaffrey, D. F., & Karam, R. (2014). Effectiveness of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I at Scale. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 36(2), 127-144. doi:10.3102/0162373713507480 (ERIC EJ1024233; addendum RAND WR-1050, ED559621)
design: cluster randomized trial, matched school pairs, 2 years
population_location: 147 middle and high schools (73 high schools) in 7 states
program_model: Cognitive Tutor Algebra I blended curriculum (textbook plus adaptive software)
direction: null year 1; positive year 2 in high schools
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'finds no effects in the first year of implementation, but finds evidence in support of positive effects in the second year. The estimated effect is statistically significant for high schools but not for middle schools'. Addendum: 'a significant positive effect of 0.21 standard deviation units for high school students in the second year'
notes: school model, not a partner link (curriculum adopted by teachers). Evidence for ESSA rates Carnegie Learning HS Math Solution Algebra I 'Strong' with weighted ES +0.04 across 3 studies.

citation: Campuzano, L., Dynarski, M., Agodini, R., & Rall, K. (2009). Effectiveness of Reading and Mathematics Software Products: Findings From Two Student Cohorts (NCEE 2009-4041). IES (ERIC ED504657).
population_location: US districts; Algebra I software arm in high schools
program_model: Algebra I software products (incl. Cognitive Tutor)
effect_as_reported: Abstract: after one year 'differences in student test scores were not statistically significant'; 'for algebra I, effects on student test scores were statistically significantly higher in the second year than in the first year.' 'One product had a positive and statistically significant effect. Nine did not'
notes: school model, not a partner link.

citation: Barrow, L., Markman, L., & Rouse, C. E. (2009). Technology's Edge: The Educational Benefits of Computer-Aided Instruction. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 1(1), 52-74 (NBER WP 14240).
population_location: Three urban US districts, pre-algebra and algebra classes (middle and high school; grade mix to confirm)
program_model: Computer-aided instruction program (I Can Learn) for pre-algebra/algebra
effect_as_reported: NBER abstract: 'Students randomly assigned to computer-aided instruction score 0.17 of a standard deviation higher on pre-algebra/algebra tests than students randomly assigned to traditional instruction.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Test not a state EOC.

citation: Heppen, J. B., Walters, K., Clements, M., Faria, A.-M., Tobey, C., Sorensen, N., & Culp, K. (2011). Access to Algebra I: The Effects of Online Mathematics for Grade 8 Students (NCEE 2012-4021). IES (ERIC ED527394; brief ED537606).
population_location: Mostly rural Maine and Vermont schools that did not offer Algebra I in grade 8; algebra-ready 8th graders
program_model: Offering an online Algebra I course (Class.com) with on-site proctor
outcome_measure: End-of-grade-8 algebra assessment; advanced HS math course sequence
effect_as_reported: Brief: 'scored higher than students in control schools on an algebra achievement test given at the end of eighth grade... 5.5 points... equivalent to moving students from the 50th to the 66th percentile'; 'equal to an effect size of 0.40 standard deviations'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Lead from task confirmed. Grade 8 but a high-school-level course, so lane 1. Contrast: online credit recovery (L-145) was negative.

citation: Cavalluzzo, L., Lowther, D. L., Mokher, C., & Fan, X. (2012). Effects of the Kentucky Virtual Schools' Hybrid Program for Algebra I on Grade 9 Student Math Achievement (NCEE 2012-4020). IES (ERIC ED530803).
population_location: Kentucky high schools, 61% rural
program_model: Hybrid online plus face-to-face Algebra I curriculum
outcome_measure: Algebra I achievement test; later course-taking
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'the hybrid class format was no more effective at increasing student achievement and future coursetaking in math than algebra offered in the traditional face-to-face format'
notes: school model, not a partner link.

citation: Chakraborty, N., Roy, S., Leite, W. L., Faradonbeh, M. K. S., & Michailidis, G. (2021). The Effects of a Personalized Recommendation System on Students' High-Stakes Achievement Scores: A Field Experiment. Educational Data Mining 2021 (ERIC ED615676).
population_location: Florida Algebra 1 students using Math Nation
program_model: Video recommendation algorithm inside the free Math Nation (Algebra Nation) platform, used in and out of school
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'effects of the recommendation algorithm depend on the level of usage of students, showing significant improvements on EoC test scores of students who have a moderate level of usage. However, there was no effect for low usage students.'
proposed_tier: Below the bar (tests a platform feature, effect only in a usage subgroup)
notes: Tests a feature, not the platform. Leite et al. 2019 (EJ1227078) on Algebra Nation usage is correlational: excluded.

citation: Dee, T. S., & Huffaker, E. (2024). Accelerating Opportunity: The Effects of Instructionally Supported Detracking. EdWorkingPaper 24-986 (ERIC ED660950; published version EJ1499404, 2026; SREE 2022 ED658597).
population_location: One California district (Stanford Sequoia collaborative), 9th graders far below grade level
program_model: Algebra I Initiative: placing low-scoring 9th graders in Algebra I with teacher training instead of pre-algebra
outcome_measure: Grade-11 math achievement; attendance; math credits
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'this reform significantly increased grade-11 math achievement (ES = 0.2 SD) without lowering the achievement of classroom peers... also increased attendance, district retention, and overall math credits.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Strong design; the support is teacher training, not a partner program.

citation: McEachin, A., Domina, T., & Penner, A. (2020). Heterogeneous Effects of Early Algebra across California Middle Schools. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 39(3), 772-800. doi:10.1002/pam.22202 (ERIC EJ1257074)
design: regression discontinuity (hundreds of schools with test-score placement cutoffs)
population_location: California middle schools
program_model: Placement in 8th-grade algebra
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Enrolling in 8th-grade algebra boosts students' enrollment in advanced math in ninth grade by 30 percentage points... Math scores in tenth grade rise by 0.05 standard deviations.'
notes: school model, not a partner link. Benefits larger where eligibility threshold set higher.

citation: Domina, T., McEachin, A., Penner, A., & Penner, E. (2015). Aiming High and Falling Short: California's Eighth-Grade Algebra-for-All Effort. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 37(3), 275-295. doi:10.3102/0162373714543685 (ERIC EJ1072750)
population_location: All California districts
program_model: Universal 8th-grade algebra
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'enrolling more students in advanced courses has negative average effects on students' achievement, driven by negative effects in large districts.'
notes: school model, not a partner link.

citation: Clotfelter, C. T., Ladd, H. F., & Vigdor, J. L. (2015). The Aftermath of Accelerating Algebra: Evidence from District Policy Initiatives. Journal of Human Resources, 50(1), 159-188 (CALDER WP 69 2012, ERIC ED529166; NBER WP 18161).
population_location: Charlotte-Mecklenburg, NC
program_model: Accelerating moderately performing students into 8th-grade algebra
outcome_measure: North Carolina Algebra I end-of-course test; Geometry and Algebra II passing
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Students affected by the acceleration initiative scored significantly lower on end-of-course tests in Algebra I, and were either no more likely or significantly less likely to pass standard follow-up courses, Geometry and Algebra II'
notes: school model, not a partner link. State Algebra I EOC outcome.

citation: Dougherty, S. M., Goodman, J. S., Hill, D. V., Litke, E. G., & Page, L. C. (2017). Objective course placement and college readiness: Evidence from targeted middle school math acceleration. Economics of Education Review, 58, 141-161. doi:10.1016/j.econedurev.2017.04.002 (NBER WP 21395; SREE 2014 ED562828)
population_location: Wake County, NC
program_model: Placement into accelerated middle school math by predicted Algebra I EOC success
outcome_measure: Later Precalculus enrollment, college readiness; earlier SREE version: test scores
direction: positive on course-taking; earlier version negative peer effects on scores
effect_as_reported: NBER abstract: 'Accelerated math placement of relatively low-skilled middle schoolers increases the fraction later enrolling in Precalculus by one-seventh'. SREE 2014: 'may experience negative effects as a result of being in a peer group of more advanced ability'
notes: school model, not a partner link.

citation: Rickles, J., Phillips, M., & Yamashiro, K. (2014). Effects of 8th Grade Algebra on High School Course-Taking and Math Achievement: Evidence from Changing Practices in a Large Urban District. SREE (ERIC ED562715); and Sorensen, N., et al. (2018). Does Readiness for Eighth-Grade Algebra Matter? SREE (ERIC ED591607).
population_location: Large urban district (LAUSD); two districts (Sorensen)
program_model: 8th-grade algebra placement
effect_as_reported: Rickles abstract: 'exposure to 8th grade algebra may improve math course-taking and completion but that these effects do not translate into statistically significant improvements in high school graduation rates'
notes: school model, not a partner link.

citation: Early, D. M., Berg, J. K., Alicea, S., Si, Y., Aber, J. L., Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2016). The Impact of Every Classroom, Every Day on High School Student Achievement: Results From a School-Randomized Trial. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 9(1), 3-29. doi:10.1080/19345747.2015.1055638 (ERIC EJ1089961)
population_location: 5 districts in Arizona, California, New York, Tennessee; grades 9-10
program_model: Instructional improvement: classroom observation, math teacher PD and benchmark mastery grading, literacy curriculum
outcome_measure: State standardized math and ELA tests
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Results provided evidence that ECED improved scores on standardized tests of math achievement, but not standardized tests of ELA achievement.' Evidence for ESSA: ES +0.14 on state math tests, rated Strong.
notes: school model, not a partner link. Code would be A1.2 practice change; useful for S12 null.

citation: Thomas, A. S., Bonner, S. M., Everson, H. T., & Somers, J. A. (2015). Leveraging the Power of Peer-Led Learning: Investigating Effects on STEM Performance in Urban High Schools. Educational Research and Evaluation, 21(7-8), 537-557. doi:10.1080/13803611.2016.1158657 (ERIC EJ1094395)
population_location: New York City urban high schools, 9th grade
program_model: Peer Enabled Restructured Classroom (PERC): trained peer tutors lead small groups in class
outcome_measure: NY Regents Integrated Algebra and Living Environment (Biology) end-of-course exams
direction: null algebra; positive biology in year 2
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'by the 2nd year of implementation, enrolment in PERC Biology increased the likelihood of passing. Similar effects were not observed for PERC Integrated Algebra'
proposed_tier: Null for S10 (single QED); S11 lead for the biology searcher
notes: Only peer-tutoring study found with a high school EOC outcome. Pass to the S11 searcher.

citation: Snipes, J. C., Holton, G. I., Doolittle, F., & Sztejnberg, L. (2006). Striving for Student Success: The Effect of Project GRAD on High School Student Outcomes in Three Urban School Districts. MDRC (ERIC ED493362).
design: comparative interrupted time series with matched comparison schools
population_location: Houston, Columbus, Atlanta high schools
program_model: Project GRAD feeder-pattern reform with college scholarships and supports
outcome_measure: Core curriculum completion, graduation, attendance, promotion; HS achievement in Houston (appendix)
direction: mixed (flagship school positive, others matched by comparison)
effect_as_reported: Abstract: at the flagship school 'a statistically significant positive impact on the proportion of students who completed a core academic curriculum on time'; at newer schools 'progress was matched by progress at the comparison high schools.'
notes: College-access program; no clear high school math test effect in abstract.

citation: Slavin, R. E., Lake, C., & Groff, C. (2009). Effective Programs in Middle and High School Mathematics: A Best-Evidence Synthesis. Review of Educational Research, 79(2), 839-911. doi:10.3102/0034654308330968 (ERIC EJ879460)
design: best-evidence synthesis of 100 randomized or matched studies (26 randomized)
population_location: US and comparable, grades 6-12
program_model: Math curricula, computer-assisted instruction, instructional-process programs
direction: near-null for curricula and CAI; positive for cooperative learning
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'Effect sizes were very small for mathematics curricula and for computer-assisted instruction. Positive effects were found for two cooperative learning programs.'
proposed_tier: Meta-analysis (mostly school models); supports not claiming curricula
notes: Lead from task confirmed. Does not cover tutoring or out-of-school programs.

citation: Cheung, A. C. K., & Slavin, R. E. (2013). The Effectiveness of Educational Technology Applications for Enhancing Mathematics Achievement in K-12 Classrooms: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Research Review, 9, 88-113. doi:10.1016/j.edurev.2013.01.001 (ERIC EJ999451); updated by Morrison, Borokhovski, Bernard & Slavin (2024), ERIC ED659234
program_model: Educational technology in math
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'educational technology applications generally produced a positive, though modest, effect (ES = +0.15)'; Morrison et al. 2024: 'a moderate effect (+0.12)'
notes: Secondary subgroup estimate not in abstract.

citation: Chang, A., Mauer, E., Wanzek, J., Kim, S., Scammacca, N., & Swanson, E. (2025). Examining the Academic Effects of Cross-Age Tutoring: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. doi:10.1007/s10648-025-09997-z (ERIC ED671581)
population_location: K-12, mixed
program_model: Cross-age peer tutoring
effect_as_reported: Abstract: 'The overall effect size was 0.34, with tutees benefiting at 0.33 and tutors at 0.39... no significant differences in impact from... subject area.'
proposed_tier: Below the bar for S10 (no high school math test subgroup)
notes: Mostly elementary tutees; included designs not limited to randomized. Wexler et al. 2015 (EJ1070890) secondary peer-mediated synthesis has 13 studies incl. single-case: excluded.
